html:
This chapter is the map for the rest of the book. It explains who sits the Medical Education Common Entrance Examination for Bachelor Level (MECEE-BL, usually just called "CEE"), how the 200 questions are spread across the syllabus, how the negative marking really works and when a guess pays, and how to spend the last four months, the last two months and the last fortnight. The five model papers that follow are built on this map, question for question.

The paper in one box
  • 200 single-best-answer MCQs, four options, 3 hours (180 minutes, 54 seconds a question), 200 marks, answered on an OMR sheet.
  • +1 for a right answer, −0.25 for a wrong one, 0 for a blank.
  • Group I (MBBS, BDS, BSc Nursing, BSc Midwifery, BASLP, B Perfusion): Zoology 40, Botany 40, Chemistry 50, Physics 50, Mental Agility Test 20.
  • Setters are told to write 50 % recall, 30 % understanding, 20 % application, with stems of at most 60 words.
  • A candidate must reach the 50th percentile of the scores to enter the merit list; a place on the list is not yet a seat.
  • Syllabus in force: MEC bachelor-level syllabus, third revision 2083-01-15 (28 April 2026). Older guides built on the second revision have different domains.

1.1 Who sits the paper, the programme groups and the eligibility rules

The examination is conducted by the Medical Education Commission (MEC) under the Medical Education Act, 2075. It is the single gateway to every bachelor-level health-science seat in Nepal — government and private, in every university and academy (TU, KU, BPKIHS, PAHS, NAMS, KAHS, Karnali and others). MEC names a cycle after the year of admission, so the papers sat from 31 October to 4 November 2026 (Kartik 14–18, 2083) belong to MECEE-BL 2027.

The four programme groups

Group Programmes Paper (200 questions)
I MBBS, BDS, BSc Nursing, BSc Midwifery, BASLP, B Perfusion Technology Zoology 40, Botany 40, Chemistry 50, Physics 50, MAT 20
II BAMS, BSc MLT, BSc MIT, BSc Radiotherapy, BPT, B Pharm, B Optometry and similar Zoology 40, Botany 40, Chemistry 40, Physics 40, programme-specific PCL content 20, MAT 20
III BPH Zoology 40, Botany 40, Chemistry 40, Physics 40, prerequisite health knowledge 20, MAT 20
IV BNS, BMS (for nurses with a PCL) nursing subjects 150, basic and integrated health science 30, MAT 20

This book follows the Group I paper, which is also the one that most +2 science students sit. A Group II or III candidate can use every chapter as it stands — the Physics and Chemistry sections are simply ten questions shorter in the real paper.

Eligibility in short

Route Usual minimum (check the year's notice)
+2 Science (NEB) or equivalent Physics, Chemistry and Biology studied; at least 50 % aggregate or CGPA 2.4
Health-science PCL/diploma (for the programmes that allow it) at least 50 % in the diploma, the Grade 12 science equivalence where required, and registration with the relevant council
BNS / BMS PCL or diploma in Nursing with at least 50 %, registered with the Nepal Nursing Council

The notice for each cycle can add conditions on subjects, equivalence, foreign qualifications and quota categories, and the dates change every year. The rules above are the stable core; the authority is always the current notice on the MEC website and the admit card, which names your centre and reporting time.

Read the notice, not a coaching poster

Dates, fees and category rules change between cycles. In the 2027 cycle the double-fee window closed in September 2026 and the MBBS paper was set for 31 October 2026, 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. — but for any later cycle, check MEC's own notice before you plan backwards from a date.

1.2 The paper: 200 questions, unit by unit, and how the marks are counted

The syllabus fixes the number of questions in every unit (area). How a unit's questions fall between its chapters is not published; the NEBians books give an estimate in each chapter, and the model papers use those estimates. The unit totals below are official.

Subject Unit (official count)
Zoology (40) Evolutionary biology 3 · Animal diversity and classification 4 · Animal tissues 4 · Plasmodium, earthworm and frog 6 · Human biology and physiology 15 · Microbial diseases and immunology 4 · Medical technology and applied biology 2 · Biota, environment and conservation 2
Botany (40) Basic components of life 2 · Biodiversity 9 · Ecology and vegetation 4 · Cell biology 5 · Genetics 6 · Plant anatomy 3 · Plant physiology 6 · Developmental botany 2 · Applied botany 3
Chemistry (50) Physical 17 · Inorganic 10 · Organic 17 · Applied 3 · Analytical 3
Physics (50) Mechanics 10 · Heat and thermodynamics 7 · Waves and optics 8 · Current electricity and magnetism 9 · Electrostatics and capacitors 4 · Modern physics 12
MAT (20) Verbal reasoning 5 · Numerical reasoning 5 · Logical sequencing 5 · Spatial relation and abstract reasoning 5

The cognitive split and what it means for you

MEC instructs setters to write about 100 recall, 60 understanding and 40 application questions. Recall questions (a name, a number, a definition, an example) are the fastest marks in the hall — ten to twenty seconds each if you know them. Application questions (a numerical, a cross, a reaction sequence) take one to two minutes. So the 54-second average is not spent evenly: a student who races through recall at 20 seconds a question banks more than an hour for the numericals.

How the score becomes a rank

  1. Raw score = right − 0.25 × wrong. Blanks score zero.
  2. Candidates at or above the 50th percentile of the scores qualify for the merit list (the notice sets a fallback — a 50 % score qualifies — for a programme with fewer than twice as many applicants as seats).
  3. The merit list is used for seat matching by rank, quota category, seat type (government scholarship or paying) and your stated preferences. A rank is not a seat until you are matched and you complete admission on time.

1.3 Negative marking and when to guess

With four options and a quarter-mark penalty, the arithmetic is simpler than most students think. If p is your chance of being right on a question, the expected mark from answering it is

E = p\times 1 - (1 - p)\times 0.25 = 1.25p - 0.25

E is positive whenever p > 0.2. A blind guess among four options has p = 0.25, so even a blind guess has a small positive expectation (E = +0.0625). Every option you can eliminate with confidence raises it sharply.

Options you can rule out p Expected mark from answering Verdict
none (blind) 1/4 +0.06 barely worth it; costs time and adds variance
one 1/3 +0.17 answer
two 1/2 +0.38 answer, always
three (you know it) 1 +1.00 answer

The trap in "a blind guess pays"

The calculation assumes that a wrong option is chosen at random. Setters build distractors from the commonest mistakes, so a half-understood question can pull your p below 0.2 — you are drawn to the trap, not to a random option. Answer when you have eliminated at least one option for a reason; skip when your "hunch" is really a vague memory of a word in one option.

Worked example 1.1 — what skipping costs

Problem. A student knows 120 answers, can eliminate two options in 40 more, and has no idea about the last 40. Compare (i) answering only the 120, (ii) answering the 160, (iii) answering all 200 at random for the last 40.

Solution. (i) 120. (ii) The 40 half-known questions add 40\times0.375 = 15 on average: about 135. (iii) The 40 blind guesses add 40\times0.0625 = 2.5 on average, but with a spread of about ±3.5 marks. Answering the half-known questions is worth fifteen marks — often thousands of places in rank. Blind guessing is close to neutral; spend that time checking instead.

Three passes through the paper

  1. First pass (≈ 90 min): answer everything you know at once; mark (on the question paper, not the OMR) questions that need work.
  2. Second pass (≈ 60 min): the marked numericals and two-step questions; eliminate options and answer where at least one is ruled out.
  3. Third pass (≈ 20 min): OMR check — every bubble in the right row, darkened completely, no stray marks — and a last look at the remaining blanks.
OMR discipline

Fill the OMR section by section (after every 20–30 questions), not all at the end and not one bubble at a time. A shifted row — answer 57 bubbled in row 58 — costs more marks than any hard question in the paper.

1.4 A study plan for the last 120, 60 and 15 days

The plans assume about 8–10 hours of study a day after +2 and the official weightage above. Adjust the share to your weak units, never to your favourite ones.

120 days out: build the base

Weeks Physics + Chemistry (100 Q) Biology (80 Q) MAT (20 Q)
1–6 Mechanics, Heat, Physical chemistry, General organic chemistry Human physiology, Plasmodium/earthworm/frog, Biodiversity 20 min a day, one area a week
7–12 Optics, Electricity and magnetism, Inorganic, Hydrocarbons to Amines Cell biology, Genetics, Plant physiology and anatomy timed sets of 20
13–17 Modern physics, Electrostatics, Applied and Analytical chemistry Evolution, Tissues, Applied zoology, Ecology, Applied botany mixed sets

Every day: one chapter's theory, then all its Set A and Set B questions, then review every wrong answer and write the fact you missed in a one-line error log.

60 days out: practise under the clock

  • One subject test (40–50 questions in 40–45 minutes) every day, rotating subjects.
  • From day 45: a full model paper every fourth day, 3 hours, OMR-style, in the morning at the real exam time (11:00 to 14:00).
  • Score every paper with the negative marking; track right, wrong and blank per unit in a table. Units with the most wrong answers get the next week's revision.

15 days out: consolidate, do not start anything new

  • Revise only from the Formula and fact sheets and Chapter summaries of the subject books and from your own error log.
  • Two full papers in the first ten days; none in the last three.
  • Sleep at the time you will sleep before the exam; travel to the centre once in advance if it is unfamiliar. Keep the admit card, a photo ID and two black/blue ballpoint pens ready the night before.
The weightage in one line

"Fifty-fifty, forty-forty, twenty": Physics 50, Chemistry 50, Zoology 40, Botany 40, MAT 20. Inside them, the giants are Human biology 15, Physical chemistry 17, Organic chemistry 17 and Modern physics 12 — 61 marks in four units.

1.5 How to use the model papers in this book

Each model paper (chapters 2–6) is a complete 200-question paper built to the official unit counts. A table at the top of each paper shows its actual count per unit. Every question is original practice written to the third-revision syllabus — none is copied from or claimed to be a past paper.

  • On the NEBians website or app, open a model paper and choose Take as a timed test: a three-hour clock that does not pause, one answer per question, a question palette, and the real marking (+1, −0.25, 0). At the end you get your score, the right/wrong/blank count, a per-subject table and every explanation.
  • On paper, print the PDF, set a timer for 180 minutes, mark answers on a separate sheet, and score with right − 0.25 × wrong.
  • After each paper, spend at least as long on the key as on the paper: for every wrong or blank answer read the explanation, find the chapter in the subject book and add the missed fact to your error log.
  • Take the papers in order and several days apart: each one tests different facts and different numbers, so later papers measure improvement, not memory.
Reading your score

On these papers, aim first for 120+ (60 %) and then for 150+. More useful than the total is the per-subject table: a section where you score under half is where the next week of study goes.

Formula and fact sheet

Item Value
Questions, time, marks 200 MCQs, 180 min, 200 marks; 54 s a question on average
Marking +1 right, −0.25 wrong, 0 blank; score = R − 0.25W
Expected value of answering E = 1.25p - 0.25; break-even p = 0.2
Blind / one out / two out +0.06 / +0.17 / +0.38 per question
Group I split Zoology 40, Botany 40, Chemistry 50, Physics 50, MAT 20
Group II/III split Physics 40 and Chemistry 40, plus 20 programme-specific
Cognitive mix recall 50 %, understanding 30 %, application 20 %; stem ≤ 60 words
Merit list 50th percentile and above (50 % score fallback for undersubscribed programmes)
Syllabus MEC third revision, 2083-01-15 (28 April 2026)

Chapter summary

  • MECEE-BL is MEC's single entrance for every bachelor-level health-science seat; the 2027 cycle's papers ran from 31 October to 4 November 2026.
  • Group I sits Zoology 40, Botany 40, Chemistry 50, Physics 50 and MAT 20; the unit counts inside each subject are official and drive every model paper here.
  • Marking is +1, −0.25, 0; answering pays whenever your chance of being right exceeds 0.2, so answer every question where you can eliminate an option for a reason.
  • A half-understood question can make you worse than random — distractors are built from common mistakes.
  • Work in three passes and fill the OMR section by section.
  • Build the base for four months, practise under the clock for two, and only consolidate in the last fortnight.
  • Use each model paper as a diagnostic: the key and the error log matter more than the score.
